JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON
1. The present batch of Appeals has been filed by Adani Power Limited
Raipur, TPP ( “Appellant”), challenging the common Order dated 20.01.2026
passed by the Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission (herein after
referred as “State Commission/CSERC”) in Petition Nos. 71 of 2025 and 72 of
2025, whereby the State Commission disallowed recovery of Fly Ash
Transportation Charges incurred pursuant to the MoEF&CC Notifications dated
25.01.2016 and 31.12.2021 and directed refund of the amounts recovered from
Chhattisgarh State Power Distribution Company Limited (CSPDCL/Respondent
no. 2), holding the same to be non-recoverable under the applicable regulatory
framework. The details of the present Appeals are set out here in below:
Description of Parties
2. The Appellant - Adani Power Limited, Raipur TPP is a generating company
in terms of Section 2(28) of the Electricity Act, 2003 and, owns and operates
Page 3 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
Thermal Power Plants (“TPP”), which in present appeals concerns Raigarh TPP
(1x600 MW) and Raipur TPP (2x685), in the State of Chhattisgarh.
3. The Respondent No. 1- CSERC is the State Electricity Regulatory
Commission in the State of Chhattisgarh with powers vested under Sections 86
and 181 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
4. The Respondent No. 2- CSPDCL is a Distribution Licensee in the State of
Chhattisgarh and is purchasing 5% of the net power generated by the Appellant’s
power projects at variable cost in terms of Power Purchase Agreement dated
09.02.2015 and 08.07.2020.
Factual matrix of the Case(s):
5. Raipur Thermal Power Plant (Subject project in Appeal 65 of 2026) is
situated in the State of Chhattisgarh. The Project comprises two generating units
of 685 MW each. Unit-I achieved Commercial Operation Date (“COD”) on
01.06.2015 and Unit-II achieved COD on 01.04.2016. The Project was
subsequently acquired by the Appellant in the year 2019 through a bidding
process initiated by Axis Bank. On 08.07.2020, the Appellant entered into a
Power Purchase Agreement (“PPA”) with Chhattisgarh State Power Distribution
Company Limited (“CSPDCL”) for supply of 5% of the net power generated from
the Project. Pursuant thereto, supply of power commenced on 21.07.2020.
6. Raigarh Thermal Power Plant (Subject project in Appeal 66 of 2026) is also
situated in the State of Chhattisgarh having an installed capacity of 600 MW. The
generating station achieved COD on 31.03.2014 and was subsequently acquired
by the Appellant through the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. On
09.02.2015, the Appellant entered into a PPA with CSPDCL for supply of 5% of
Page 4 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
the net power generated from the Project. Supply of power under the said
arrangement commenced on 01.05.2015.
7. Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (“MoEF&CC”) issued
Notifications dated 25.01.2016 and 31.12.2021 prescribing mandatory
obligations relating to disposal and utilisation of fly ash generated from thermal
power stations. The Notifications, inter alia, stipulated progressive utilization of fly
ash and imposed obligations upon thermal power generators for transportation
and utilization of fly ash in accordance with the prescribed environmental norms.
8. Following the issuance of the aforesaid Notifications, Appellant has claimed
to incur additional expenditure incurred towards handling, transportation and
utilization of fly ash for compliance with the statutory requirements.
9. On 14.02.2025, the Appellant raised a supplementary invoice upon
CSPDCL for an amount of Rs.1,09,72,560/-(Rupees One Crore Nine Lakh
Seventy-Two Thousand Five Hundred and Sixty Only) for Raipur Thermal Project
and for Rs.1,85,94,781/- (Rupees One Crore Eighty Five Lakhs Ninety Four
Thousand Seven Hundred Eighty One Only) for Raigarh Project for the payment
of additional expenses incurred by the Appellant towards handling, transportation
and utilization of fly ash for FY 2022-23 and FY 2023-24.
10. On 28.02.2025 CSPDCL disputed the claim made on the ground that fly
ash transportation and utilization expenses formed part of Operation and
Maintenance (“O&M”) expenses and were not recoverable under the PPA, as
CSPDCL was procuring power only at variable charges. Notwithstanding its
objections, CSPDCL subsequently released payment of the aforesaid amount
under protest.
Page 5 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
11. Aggrieved by the claims raised by the Appellant, Respondent No.2-
CSPDCL on 04.10.25 filed Petition No.72 of 2025 for Raipur Project and Petition
No.71 of 2025 for Raigarh Project before the State Commission seeking, inter
alia, a declaration that fly ash transportation and utilization expenses formed part
of fixed cost/O&M expenses and were not recoverable from CSPDCL, together
with refund of the amounts already paid along with Carrying cost.
12. On 16.10.2025, Appellant raised another supplementary invoice for
Rs.99,20,346/- for Raipur Project and Rs.1,30,44,960/- for Raigarh Project
towards similar expenditure incurred during FY 2024-25.
13. State Commission passed the common Order dated 20.01.2026 in Petition
Nos.71 of 2025 and 72 of 2025, (impugned order) and held that fly ash utilization
expenses were recoverable only through fixed charges, and directed refund of
the amounts already recovered by the Appellant together with applicable interest.
14. Aggrieved by the findings and directions contained in the common Order
dated 20.01.2026, the Appellant has preferred the present batch of Appeals.
Analysis and Discussion
15. Since the issues involved in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 and 66 of 2026 arise
out of a common Impugned Order dated 20.01.2026 and involve identical
questions of fact and law, both the Appeals were heard together and are being
disposed of by this common judgment. Heard Mr Amit Kapur, learned Counsel for
the Appellant, Mr Buddy Ranganathan, learned senior Counsel appearing on
behalf of Discoms, Ms Swapna Sheshadri, learned Counsel on behalf of State
Page 6 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
Commission, perused written submissions filed by parties, Impugned Order and
other documents on record.
16. The State Commission, in the Impugned Order after noting the definition
of change in law as per of MYT Regulations 2021, Notifications and Change in
Law Rules, in paragraph 41 observed that “keeping in view the above
definitions, the notifications of MOEF&CC dated 25.01.2016 and 31.12.2021
are coming under the purview of Change in Law”. With regard to applicability
of such change in law in the case of Appellant herein, in paragraph 52, it is held
that “any expenses towards ash Utilisation are required to be recovered
through fixed charges only” and Appellant is not entitled to recover the same
from the Discom and ordered refund of the payment, already received by
Appellant, to the Discoms along with interest.
17. It has been contended by Appellant that in light of the judgment of the
Supreme Court in “PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission” (2010) 4 SCC 603 ("PTC Judgment"), it is a settled position of
law that statutory provisions override contractual stipulations, including the terms
of a PPAs. Further the phrase "variable cost only" contained in PPA was intended
merely to define the commercial billing structure for supply and did not impose an
absolute bar on the recovery of statutory expenses. The Appellant has further
relied upon the second proviso to Regulation 40.5.2.1 of the MYT Regulations,
2021, which expressly provides for pass-through of expenses arising from
compliance with statutory directions, including fly ash transportation/utilization
expenses, over and above routine O&M expenses. Moreover, while O&M
expenses are incurred within the project premises, even during periods of no
generation, fly ash transportation/utilization expenses are incurred outside the
project premises and vary directly with the quantum of generation, thereby
Page 7 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
making them variable in nature. Article 19.5 of the PPA, provides that
notwithstanding anything contained in the PPA, if any provision thereof is
inconsistent with the provisions of the Electricity Act or the Rules and Regulations
framed thereunder, such provision shall be deemed to be amended to the extent
required to bring about such consistency. The State Commission has also failed
to consider various judgments of this Tribunal in Appeal No. 109 of 2022 dated
07.08.2025 and Appeal No. 345 of 2021 dated 08.05.2025, despite Appellant’s
specific reliance upon the same during the course of hearing before State
Commission as well as CERC order dated 22.12.2023 in Petition No.
202/MP/2022. By ignoring binding precedent, the Impugned Order violates the
principle of judicial consistency. In particular, the Order dated 22.12.2023 passed
by CERC which specifically recognizes the recovery of fly ash transportation
charges separately from O&M expenses and Annual Fixed Charges.
18. Per Contra, it has been contended on behalf of Respondents that CSERC
MYT Regulations, 2021 have undergone multiple amendments subsequent to the
issuance of the 2021 MoEF&CC Notification concerning fly ash disposal, and
provisions in the Regulation clearly demonstrates that fly ash cost component is
included as part of fixed cost. The Regulation 45.5 of the CSERC MYT
Regulations, 2021, which prescribes the methodology for determination of
variable charges, also does not include expenditure incurred towards fly ash
utilization within its ambit. Further, pass-through of fly ash transportation
expenses has also been specifically qualified in the MoEF& CC notification dated
31.12.2021 itself, as Statutory obligation of 100 percent utilization of ash to be
treated as change in law, wherever applicable. It is thus evident that there is no
scope for any blanket recognition of the said notifications as Change in Law
events, as such an interpretation contrary to the terms of the PPAs is neither
envisaged under the notifications nor change in Law Rules. The expenses
Page 8 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
relating to fly ash utilization are components of fixed cost and do not form part of
variable charges. Therefore, in the absence of any provision under the PPA
permitting payment of fixed cost expenses or any Change in Law expenses, the
Respondent is not bound to pay the expenses incurred by the Appellant towards
fly ash handling, disposal and transportation.
19. There is no dispute that considering the Change in Law provision in
Regulation 3.14 of the MYT Regulation 2021 and Rule 2 (c) of Electricity Rules
2021, the notifications of MOEF&CC dated 25.01.2016 and 31.12.2021 shall
come under the purview of Change in Law, as noted in the Impugned Order.
Applicability of same in the present case is deliberated in following Paragraphs
Provision of PPA
Under the PPAs, Appellant is supplying 30 MW power from Raigarh TPP and 63
MW from Raipur TPP. Terms of both the PPAs are identical, and relevant
provisions from PPA dated 08.07.2020 for Raipur TPP are extracted hereunder.
“Article 1.1 (Definitions)
“Tariff” shall mean the Energy Charge/Variable Charge/Variable cost as
determined in accordance with the relevant regulations of CERC from time to
time and approved by the Appropriate Commission or the
Consultant/Committee as per Article 8.1, as the case may be”
Article 8.1 (Applicable Tariff)
“8.1.1 Both the Parties agree that the Tariff for supply of the Contracted
Energy to CSPTradeco from the Generating Station of the Company under
this Agreement shall be determined in accordance with CERC Regulations
from time to time and approved by the Appropriate Commission and shall be
calculated as per Schedule-6 hereof.”
Article 14 (Change in Law
Page 9 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
“14.1 The parties agree that the Variable charges being determined by the
Appropriate Commission based on actual at the relevant time and there being
no aspect of capacity or fixed charges payment under this agreement, there
shall be no implication of the changes in law and no provision need to be
made for the said purpose.”
19.5 Compliance with Law
“Despite anything contained in this Agreement, if any provision of this
Agreement shall be in deviation or inconsistent with or repugnant to the
provisions contained in the Electricity Act, 2003, or any rules and regulations
made there under, such provision shall be deemed to be amended to the
extent required to bring it into compliance with the aforesaid relevant
provisions as amended from time to time.”
Provisions Under MYT Regulation 2021
20. Regulation 37 of MYT Regulations 2021 provides for the component of
Annual Fixed Charges, in which under O&M expenses, Maintenance & General
(M&G) Expenses are included. Under Regulation 40.5.2, defining M&G
expenses, following is provided under 2nd Proviso:
“Provided that in all cases the additional O & M cost incurred due to any
change/compliance of law or any direction by in statutory authority including
but not limited to expenses on ash utilisation (not covered in additional
capitalisation) shall be pass through over and above the O & M charges
allowed in tariff order”
MOEF & CC notification dated 31.12.2021
Clause A (10)
Statutory obligation of 100 percent utilisation of ash shall be treated as a
change in law, wherever applicable
21. In view of above contentions raised, and the provisions of PPA, the
applicable Regulations and MOEF&CC notification, following issue emerges for
consideration:
Page 10 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
Whether, in view of the provisions of the Power Purchase Agreement, the
Appellant stands barred from seeking restitution under the doctrine of
Change in Law on account of the Notifications issued by the Ministry of
Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and whether the Appellant is
entitled to recover from Respondent No. 2 (the Distribution Licensee), the
charges incurred towards transportation and disposal of fly ash as a
consequence of such statutory notifications?”
22. The doctrine of “Change in Law” is a well-recognized principle in regulatory
jurisprudence, signifying the occurrence of a legislative enactment, subordinate
legislation, regulation, notification, or binding judicial pronouncement,
subsequent to the finalization of contractual arrangement between the parties
including the cut-off date if any stipulated, which materially alters the legal
position governing the rights and obligations of the contracting parties. The
essence of the doctrine lies in ensuring that no party is unfairly prejudiced by
supervening legal developments beyond its control. Accordingly, where a Change
in Law event imposes additional financial burden, restricts performance, or
otherwise modifies the contractual equilibrium, the affected party is entitled to
restitutionary relief so as to restore it to the same economic position as if such
change had not occurred. The principle thus operates as a shield against
unforeseen statutory or regulatory interventions, mandating that the
consequences of such change be equitably allocated, thereby preserving the
sanctity of contract and ensuring that the party impacted by the Change in Law
is duly compensated or relieved to the extent of such impact.
23. In the present case, admittedly, the Appellant supplies power only on
variable cost, essentially covering actual fuel charges, and seems to have
Page 11 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
consciously agreed not to pass fixed costs to the Respondents, including O&M
charges which also includes ash handling charges. However, it is also a fact that
Ash is produced only when power is generated. Thus, the burden arises directly
from generation activity. In our view, by agreeing to supply power only on variable
charges to the Respondent, Appellant after considering the known fixed cost
including the O&M costs in generation of electricity at the time of signing of the
PPA, agreed to bear the same. However, MoEF &CC Notifications imposes
additional expenditure on ash utilisation. This notification is a statutory
instrument, acknowledged as Change in Law under Rule 2(c) of the Electricity
Rules 2021 and Regulation 3.14 of MYT Regulations, 2021 as also noted in the
Impugned Order and not challenged.
24. The doctrine of Change in Law is not confined to the nomenclature of fixed
or variable charges, but is anchored in the broader principle of restitution. Its
object is to restore the affected party to the same economic position as if such
change had not occurred. Thus, even where the incidence of Change in Law is
reflected in the variable component of tariff, or arises as a derivative of fixed cost
obligations, the entitlement of the impacted party to relief cannot be denied. The
classification of tariff elements into fixed and variable is a matter of regulatory
design, but the underlying doctrine of Change in Law operates across both,
ensuring that unforeseen statutory or regulatory impositions do not distort the
contractual equilibrium. To hold otherwise would defeat the very purpose of the
doctrine, which is to neutralize the economic consequences of supervening legal
developments and thereby preserve fairness and sanctity of contract. Thus in the
present case, that Appellant has and is liable to incur extra cost on account of
ash utilization in terms of MOEF&CC notification dated 26.12.2021, which being
recognized as change in law, gets entitled to restitution.
Page 12 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
25. The Reliance has been placed by Respondents on Hon'ble Supreme Court
judgement in “Haryana Power Purchase Centre v. Sasan Power Ltd. and
Ors.” (2024) 1 SCC 247 and “Chamundeshwari Electricity Supply Company
Ltd. v. Saisudhir Energy Chitradurga (Pvt.) Ltd. and Anr.” 2025 SCC OnLine
SC 1816 , to contend that the PPA has to be enforced strictly in accordance with
its express stipulations. The Respondents have also contended that Electricity
“Electricity Rules 2021”, specifically recognizes contractual exclusions while
determining the entitlement to Change in Law relief. In support of the said
contention, the Respondents have relied upon the relevant definition contained
in the Electricity Rules, 2021, which is extracted hereinbelow:
“2. De initions.— (1) In these rules, unless the context otherwise
requires,—
…
(c) “change in law”, in relation to tariff, unless otherwise de ined in the
agreement, means any enactment or amendment or repeal of any law,
made after the determination of tariff under section 62 or section 63
of the Act, leading to corresponding changes in the cost requiring change in
tariff, and includes—
(i) a change in interpretation of any law by a competent court; or
(ii) a change in any domestic tax, including duty, levy, cess, charge or
surcharge by the Central Government, State Government or Union
territory administration leading to corresponding changes in the
cost; or
(iii) a change in any condition of an approval or license obtained or to be
obtained for purchase, supply or transmission of electricity, unless
speci ically excluded in the agreement for the purchase, supply
or transmission of electricity, which results in any change in the
cost,………”
26. In the present case, under Article 14.1 of the PPA, it is stipulated that since
the power is purchased at variable cost, which is being determined by the
Appropriate Commission based on actual at the relevant time and there being no
aspect of capacity or fixed charges payment under this agreement, there shall be
no implication of the changes in law and no provision need to be made for the
Page 13 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
said purpose. Thus, exclusion of change in law claim seems to be premised on
the fact that since variable charges shall be on actual to be determined by the
Commission at relevant time, there will be no implication of change in law. It can
therefore be derived that Appellant has not assumed the responsibility of
absorbing any liability which may occur on account of change in law. Thus, in our
view there is no specific exclusion/prohibition for claiming restitution under
change in law. In view of MoEF&CC notification, there is an impact of additional
charges on ash utilization, as and when power is produced for the Respondents,
Change in Law doctrine would entitle the Appellant for restitution.
27. Furthermore, although the Article 14.1 of the PPA stipulates that there shall
be no implication of Change in Law under the Agreement, however, Article 19.5
of the PPA, as noted above, operates as a saving clause with overriding effect. It
stipulates that notwithstanding any contractual provision, if there is inconsistency
between the PPA and the Electricity Act, 2003 or the subordinate legislation
framed thereunder, the PPA shall stand amended to the extent necessary to bring
about conformity. This clause is not ornamental but substantive, ensuring that the
contractual framework remains subservient to statutory mandates. It thereby
secures the supremacy of law over private bargains, and obliges the parties to
read the PPA in harmony with the governing statute and regulations. The MYT
Regulations, 2021, framed under Section 181 of the Electricity Act, expressly
recognize that additional O&M costs incurred due to compliance with statutory
directions, including fly ash utilisation, shall be a pass-through over and above
the O&M charges allowed in the tariff order. This statutory recognition cannot be
negated by the exclusionary language of Article 14.1 of the PPA, which is
contended to exclude Change in Law compensation. By virtue of Article 19.5,
the PPA must be read as incorporating the statutory entitlement, and any contrary
contractual stipulation must yield to the regulation. The Supreme Court in “PTC
Page 14 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
India Ltd. v. CERC”, (2010) 4 SCC 603 has categorically affirmed that
regulations framed under Section 178/181 have binding force and override
inconsistent contractual terms.
28. The reliance placed by Respondents on the judgments of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in “Haryana Power Purchase Centre v. Sasan Power Ltd”.
and “Chamundeshwari Electricity Supply Company Ltd. v. Saisudhir
Energy Chitradurga (Pvt.) Ltd”. is misplaced. Those decisions reiterate the
sanctity of contract in the absence of overriding statutory compulsion. In the
present case, however, the Notification dated 31.12.2021 issued by MoEF&CC
constitutes a statutory mandate under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It
is well settled that statutory provisions prevail over contractual stipulations where
the two are in conflict. The Electricity Rules 2021, while recognizing contractual
exclusions, cannot be construed to nullify statutory obligations. Accordingly, the
expenses incurred towards fly ash disposal and utilization, being a direct
consequence of a statutory notification, qualify as a Change in Law event and
must be restituted in accordance with the statutory framework, notwithstanding
contractual allocation of charges.
29. Accordingly, we are of the view that whether the burden manifests in fixed
cost or variable charge as per regulatory scheme, the affected party is entitled to
restitutionary adjustment so as to maintain parity with the pre-change economic
position, unless expressly prohibited in the agreement. We refrain from making
any observation with regard to the no Change in Law claim of the Appellant in
other PPAs, as contended by the Respondents, since the same is not under
challenge before us.
Page 15 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
30. The Appellant has relied upon the judgment of this Tribunal dated
08.05.2025 in Appeal No. 345 of 2021 and Judgement dated 07.08. 2025,
wherein it was held that the Notification dated 31.12.2021 and 25.01.2016
respectively, issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change,
imposing additional obligations upon generating companies in respect of
transportation and utilization of fly ash, constitutes a Change in Law events,
thereby entitling generators to restitutionary relief for the additional financial
burden so imposed. There is no dispute in the present case that the said
Notification qualifies as a Change in Law event. The Respondents have not
contested this position, and indeed the Impugned Order also proceeds on the
footing that the Notification dated 31.12.2021 is a Change in Law.
31. Before summarising the issues, it is to take note that both the Appellant and
the Respondents have placed reliance on certain orders of the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (CERC). The Appellant has cited the CERC’s Order
dated 22.12.2023 in Petition No. 202/MP/2022 to contend that it recognizes
recovery of fly ash transportation charges separately from O&M charges,
whereas the Respondents have relied upon the CERC’s Order dated 05.11.2018
in Petition No. 172/MP/2016 and Order dated 28.10.2022 in Petition No.
205/MP/2021, which classified fly ash transportation cost as additional O&M
expenses. It is well settled that the CERC, while exercising its adjudicatory
powers under Section 79 of the Electricity Act, 2003, functions as a statutory
tribunal of first instance. Its orders and pronouncements, though binding upon the
parties to the lis until set aside, do not constitute binding precedent upon this
Appellate Tribunal. The jurisdiction of this Tribunal under Section 111 of the
Electricity Act,2003 is appellate in nature, and while a judicial pronouncement of
the CERC cited by an appellant or respondent may have persuasive value, it
cannot fetter the independent adjudicatory discretion of this Tribunal. Binding
Page 16 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
precedent upon this Tribunal emanates only from the judgments of the Hon’ble
Supreme Court under Article 141 of the Constitution of India, and from the High
Courts within their territorial jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227. Accordingly,
we find it unnecessary to deliberate upon the CERC orders relied upon by either
party, save to note that they may be of persuasive relevance but do not control
the outcome of the present adjudication, which must be determined on the basis
of statutory provisions, binding precedent, and the contractual framework under
consideration.
32. In view of the above deliberation, we hold that Appellant is entitled to seek
restitution under the doctrine of Change in Law on account of the Notifications
issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and
consequently it is entitled to recover the charges incurred towards transportation
and disposal of fly ash as a consequence of such statutory notifications from
Respondent No. 2(CSPDCL).
33. It has been contended by the Respondents, and duly noted in the Impugned
Order, that the Appellant never sought reimbursement of expenses towards ash
disposal or transport/handling charges for fly ash in its tariff petitions filed
subsequent to the MoEF&CC Notification dated 31.12.2021. In this regard,
reliance has been placed upon Rule 1(c) of the “Electricity Rules 2021” which
defines “Change in Law” as any event occurring after the determination of tariff
under Section 62 or Section 63 of the Electricity Act 2003. The Respondents
contended that since the Appellant excluded fly ash expenses from multiple tariff
petitions filed after the notification, it failed to meet the strict procedural
requirements prescribed under the Rules. Per contra, Appellants, placing reliance
on the Electricity Rules, 2021 notified by the Ministry of Power on 22.10.2021,
have contended that since the Rules were issued after execution of the PPAs,
Page 17 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
compliance with the MoEF&CC notifications constitutes a Change in Law under
the PPAs in terms of the said Rules.
34. In this regard, we note that these submissions agitated on behalf of the
Respondents are beyond the pleadings of the parties before the Commission as
well as the contentions raised before the Commission during the hearing of the
petition. The petition Nos.71/2025 and 72/2025, in which the common order
dated 20.01.2026, which has been impugned in these two appeals, was passed
were filed by the Respondent no.2, CSPDCL claiming following reliefs: -
“Petition No.71/2025: -
i. To hold and declare that the expenses towards fly ash disposal/utilization
forms part of fixed cost expense under the provisions of the MY
Regulations, 2021;
ii. To direct the respondent to reimburse amount of Rs. 1,85,94,781/-
illegally recovered by it from the petitioner along with interest;
iii. To direct the respondent to pay carrying cost to petitioner on the amount
of Rs. 1,85,94,781/- from the date when such amount was recovered
illegally form petitioner;
iv. To direct the respondent to bear cost of the instant petition.”
Petition No.72/2025: -
i. To hold and declare that the expenses towards fly ash
disposal/utilization forms part of fixed cost expense under the provisions
of the MY Regulations, 2021;
ii. To direct the respondent to reimburse amount of Rs. 1,09,72,560/-
illegally recovered by it from the petitioner along with interest;
iii. To direct the respondent to pay carrying cost to petitioner on the amount
of Rs. 1,09,72,560/- from the date when such amount was recovered
illegally form petitioner;
iv. To direct the respondent to bear cost of the instant petition.”
Page 18 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
35. Thus, the Respondent No.2, CSPDCL, had approached the Commission
with the prayer that the expenses towards fly ash disposal/utilization may be
declared to be forming part of fixed cost expenditure under the provisions of MYT
Regulations, 2021 and to direct the Appellant to reimburse the amounts which
had been paid to the Appellant on these counts along with carrying cost. It was
nowhere contended in the petitions that the Appellant had failed to meet the
procedural requirements prescribed under the Electricity Rules, 2021 for claiming
relief under the change in law event. It is for this reason that the only issue framed
by the Commission for its consideration in Paragraph No.17 was with regards to
entitlement of the Appellant to recover fly ash disposal/transportation charges
from the Respondent No.2 due to change in law event. We find it apposite to
extract Paragraph no.18 of the impugned order of the Commission hereunder:
“18. Now, on the basis of above-mentioned facts described in petitions, replies
and rejoinders, we have to decide mainly the issue referred below:
Whether the respondent is entitled to recover fly ash disposal/
transportation charges from the petitioner due to change in law
event?”
36. Upon taking note of the rival submissions of the parties and perusal of the
relevant contractual as well as statutory provisions, the Commission concluded
as under:-
“52. From the above discussion we conclude that:
(1) Any expenses towards ash utilization are required to be recovered
through Fixed Charge only. Hence the respondent to not entitled to
recover it from the petitioner;
(2) Amount of Rs. 1,85,94,781/- as claimed in petition No. 71 of 2025 and
amount of Rs. 1,09,72,560/- as claimed in petition No. 72 of 2025, which
has been recovered by the respondent is refundable to the petitioner;
(3) The respondent is liable to pay interest at the rate, which is applicable
to the outstanding dues uploaded on the PRAAPTI portal. The interest
Page 19 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
should be calculated from the date on which the amount has been
recovered from the petitioner;
(4) The amount of Rs. 1,30,44,960/- as referred in petition No. 71 of 2025
and amount of Rs. 99,20,346/- as referred in petition No. 72 of 2025 are
posted on PRAAPTI portal, for which the petitioner prayed for stay; if has
been recovered from the petitioner, may be refundable with interest as
per order mentioned above in sub para 1 and 2 of this para;
(5) The respondent is liable to reimburse the petition fee paid by the
petitioner in both the petitions;
(6) The respondent is also liable to pay Rs. 50,000/- for each petition
regarding expenses occurred to the petitioner;”
37. Thus, the Commission decided the issue framed by it against the Appellant
herein and in favour of the Respondent No.2, which decision we have found
erroneous and not sustainable as discussed hereinabove.
38. Therefore, we do not find it necessary to discuss any other contention
raised on behalf of the Respondent No.2 in this appeal which was never raised
before the Commission and which is dehors the pleadings of the parties before
the Commission. It is a trite law that first appeal is continuation of the original
proceedings and therefore, the first appellate court is bound to base its conclusion
on the pleadings of the parties before the original court/forum as well as the
contentions raised by the parties before the same. The Respondent No. 2 cannot
be permitted to raise any fresh plea or contention in the appeal which was not
raised before the Commission during the hearing of the petition. Therefore, all
such contentions raised by the Respondent No.2 herein stand rejected outrightly.
Page 20 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 65 of 2026 & 66 of 2026
Conclusion
In view of above deliberations, the Impugned Order is set aside on the issue
raised in this Appeal. We hold that MOEF&CC Notification dated 31.12.2021,
being Change in Law event, Appellant is entitled to restitutionary adjustment so
as to maintain parity with the pre-change economic position. We further hold that
the Commission has erred in observing in the impugned order that expenses
towards ash utilization are required to be recovered through fixed charges only.
We hold that the Appellant is entitled to recover such expenses towards ash
utilization from the Discom i.e. Respondent No.2. Accordingly, the direction
issued in the impugned order to the Appellant to refund the amounts received by
it from the Respondent No.2 also stands quashed. The conclusion of the
Commission in the Impugned Order that the Appellant is liable to reimburse the
petition fee to Respondent No.2 and to pay expenses of Rs.50,000/- for each
petition , is also hereby quashed.
The Captioned appeals and pending IAs are disposed of in above terms.
PRONOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT ON THIS 29th DAY OF JULY, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

(Appellate Jurisdiction)

Email: cences@tnebnet.org … Respondent (s)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 1 of 33

Counsel for the Appellant(s) : Anand K. Ganesan
Swapna Seshadri
Ashwin Ramanathan
Damodar Solanki
for App. 1
Counsel for the Respondent(s) : Anusha Nagarajan
For Res. 2 & 3
J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. In this appeal, the Appellant has assailed the order dated 2nd
February, 2021 passed by the 1st Respondent – Tamil Nadu Electricity
Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”) in
DRP No. 8 of 2020 filed by the Appellant thereby refusing to grant project
specific extension of the Commercial Operation Date (COD) of the
Appellant’s solar power project. The Commission has also held that since
the Appellant’s power project was not commissioned within 34 months
from 26th September, 2017 (date of signing of the PPA between it and
the 2nd Respondent), the PPA stood automatically terminated and the 2nd
Respondent is entitled to relief provided under Article use 14 of the PPA
to the extent of non-commissioning of the power project by the Appellant.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 2 of 33

2. The Appellant is a company registered under Companies Act, 2013
and is engaged in the business of solar power generation as well as other
allied activities.
3. Respondent No. 2 – Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution
Corporation Limited (TANGEDCO) is the sole distribution licensee in the
State of Tamil Nadu.
4. Brief facts of the case, relevant for the disposal of the instant
appeal, are that 2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO issued a tender in the
year 2017 for procurement of total capacity of 1500 MW of solar power
from the developers on long-term basis. The tender was prepared and
issued in line with the “Guidelines for tariff based competitive bidding
process for procurement of power from grid connected solar PV power
projects, 2017” dated 3rd August, 2017 issued by the Ministry of Power,
Government of India as a guiding principle.
5. The Appellant also participated in the tender and was declared L-1
bidder having quoted Rs.3.47 per unit. Accordingly, Letter of Intent (LOI)
dated 28th August, 2017 was issued by 2nd Respondent to the Appellant.
As required under clause 5.0 of the LOI, the Appellant furnished two
Performance Bank Guarantees for a total amount of Rs.20 crores and
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 3 of 33

also entered into Power Purchase Agreement dated 26th September,
2017 with the 2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO for a period of 25 years.
6. As per clause 14 of the PPA, the Appellant had to commission its
power project by 25th September, 2019 i.e. within 24 months from the
date of the signing of the PPA.
7. Vide notification dated 30th July, 2018, the Ministry of Finance
imposed a “Safeguard Duty” (in short “SGD”) on the modules and solar
panels to be imported from all developed countries such as China,
Taiwan and Malaysia. The notification imposed safeguard duty beyond
25% on the advolerum value of the modules thereby increasing the price
of modules by 25%.
8. The 2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO was duly informed about the
imposition of safeguard duty by the Appellant vide letter dated 8th March,
2019 with the request to revise the tariff payable for the Appellant’s power
project, which was rejected by the 2nd Respondent vide reply dated 15th
May, 2019.
9. Subsequently, vide letter dated 28th June, 2019 addressed to the
2nd Respondent, the Appellant requested for confirmation of part
commissioning of the solar power projects as it had arrangement to
ensure 50% of the total PPA capacity to be ready for commissioning. Vide
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 4 of 33

another letter sent on the same date, the Appellant sought permission to
evacuate power through 33/110kv level instead of 230kv level in order
to expedite and complete the project. The 2nd Respondent vide reply
dated 23rd July, 2019 informed the Appellant that request for part
commissioning would be considered but refused to allow the petitioner to
evacuate power through 33/110kv level instead of 230kv level.
10. Thereafter, the Appellant sent two letters to the 2nd Respondent
seeking extension of COD of the power project on the ground of sudden
imposition of safeguard duty modules imported by the Appellant, but did
not receive any response to the same.
11. Feeling aggrieved by the refusal of 2nd Respondent TANGEDCO
to extend COD of the solar power project by 6 months, the Appellant
approached the Commission with the petition being DRP No. 8 of 2020
seeking following prayers :-
“In view of the above, it is humbly prayed that this Hon'ble
Court may be pleased to:
a. Grant the Petitioner a project specific extension of the
COD by fifteen (15) months in respect of the Petitioner's
SPG under PPA dated 26.09.2019 and thereby quash the
letters dated 15.05.2019; 22.05.2019 and 23.07.2019;
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 5 of 33

b. Direct the 1 and 2nd Respondents to not encash the
bank guarantees furnished by the Petitioner pursuant to
the PPA dated 26.09.2017;
c. Pass such further or other orders that this Hon'ble
Commission may deem fit in the facts and circumstances
of the case.”
12. The petition has been disposed of by the Commission vide order
dated 2nd February, 2021 which has been impugned in this appeal. The
Commission has concluded as under :-
“7.17.12. In this case, it is clear that the petitioner's project
was not commissioned within 34 months from the date of
signing PPA. Therefore, the PPA shall stand automatically
terminated as per the terms of the PPA and respondent is
entitled to the relief provided in clause 14 of the PPA to the
extent of non-commissioning of the project.
7.17.13. Accordingly, the plea for extension of date of
commissioning is rejected for the reasons stated supra.
In the result, the petition is dismissed. No costs.”
13. It appears that during the pendency of the petition before the
Commission, the 2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO had encashed the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 6 of 33

Performance Bank Guarantees amounting to Rs.15 crores submitted by
the Appellant. Accordingly, as per the submissions of the Learned
Counsel for the Appellant, the scope of the instant appeal is limited to the
question whether the 2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO is entitled to the
amounts corresponding to the Bank Guarantees submitted by the
Appellant.
14. We have heard Mr. Anand K. Ganesan, Learned Counsel for the
Appellant and Ms. Anusha Nagarajan appearing for Respondent Nos. 2
& 3. We have also perused the written submission filed by the Learned
Counsels.
15. Having regard to the submissions made by the Appellant’s Counsel
that the scope of the appeal now stands limited to the issue as to whether
the 2nd Respondent was entitled to appropriate amounts corresponding
to the Bank Guarantees submitted by the Appellant, we find that articles
14 & 15 of the PPA are relevant for discussion on this issue which are
extracted hereinbelow :-
“14 (a) Part Commissioning :
As per terms and conditions of the tender specification,
Part Commissioning will be applicable to your project.
However, Part Commissioning will be accepted by the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 7 of 33

Distribution Licensee for minimum of 50% of the plant
capacity (location wise).
b) Commissioning Schedule and Liquidated Damages for
Delay in Commissioning: The solar power plant shall be
commissioned on or before 24 months i.e. 25.09.2019
from the date of signing of this Power Purchase
Agreement. In case of failure to achieve this milestone,
Distribution Licensee shall encash the Performance
Guarantee in the following manner:
Delay up to five months. The Distribution Licensee will
encash the Performance Guarantee on per day basis
proportionate to the capacity not commissioned within (5
months after the expiry of commissioning schedule of 24
months. In case of non-commissioning within the said 29
months, the distribution licensee will encash the entire
(100%) performance bank guarantee.
Delay beyond 29 months: In case the commissioning of
project is further delayed beyond 29 months and up to 34
months, the SPG shall in addition to 100% encashment
of performance bank guarantee shall pay a liquidated
damages to the distribution licensee a sum of Rs.
10,000/-per MWac on a per day basis in the form of BG
to the extent of capacity not commissioned.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 8 of 33

Prior to expiry of 29 months from the date of signing of
PPA the SPG shall furnish an additional performance
bank guarantee calculated at Rs. 10,000/- per MWac for
5 months to the distribution licensee to the extent of
capacity not commissioned. In case of non-furnishing of
additional performance bank guarantee the PPA shall
stand terminated automatically without any notice or
order.
The Maximum time period allowed for commissioning of
the full project capacity with encashment of performance
bank guarantee and payment of liquidated damages shall
be 34 months from the date of signing of the PPA. The
amount of liquidated damages shall be recovered by
TANGEDCO from the payments due of project developer
on account of sale of solar power to TANGEDCO. In case
the commissioning of the project is delayed beyond 34
months from the date of signing of PPA the PPA capacity
shall stand reduced or amended to the extent of project
capacity commissioned when the PPA for the balance
capacity not commissioned will stand terminated and
shall be reduced from the selected project capacity. In
case the project is not commissioned within the said 34
months the PPA will stand terminated automatically
without any notice or order and the distribution licensee
will encash the performance guarantee furnished towards
liquidated damages.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 9 of 33

15. Commercial Operation Date:
The projects commissioned during the month shall be
considered for payment of energy at 50% of the PPA tariff
as infirm power till commercial operation date CODs. The
COD shall be considered 30 days from the actual date if
commissioning of the first part capacity.”
16. It is admitted case by both the parties that the PPA was executed
between the Appellant and 2nd Respondent on 26th September, 2017 and,
therefore, the Appellant ought to have commissioned the solar power
project by 25th September, 2019 i.e. within 24 months from the date of
the signing of the PPA. As per the said provision in the PPA, if the
commissioning of the project is delayed beyond 24 months from the
signing of the PPA and up to 29 months, the Distribution Licensees is
entitled to encash the performance Bank Guarantee on per day basis
proportionate to the capacity not commissioned during those five
months. In case of non-commissioning of the power project within 29
months from the date of signing of the PPA the Distribution Licensees
would be entitled to encash entire 100% of the Bank Guarantees and the
solar power generator shall also be liable to pay liquidated damages to
the DISCOM in the sum of Rs.10,000/- per MW ac on a per day basis to
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 10 of 33

the extent of capacity not commissioned. Further, in case the project is
not commissioned within 34 months from the signing of the PPA, the
PPA shall stand automatically terminated without any notice or order.
17. In this case, concededly the Appellant did not commission the
power project within 34 months from the date of the signing of the PPA
and, therefore, the 2nd Respondent became entitled to encash the entire
Performance Bank Guarantee submitted by the Appellant and the
Appellant also become liable to pay liquidated damages as per Article 14
of the PPA.
18. It has been argued on behalf of the Appellant that the 2nd
Respondent did not suffer any loss due to non-commissioning of the
power project by the Appellant and hence the respondent is liable to
refund the amounts of Bank Guarantee to the Appellant. It is submitted
that the contentions in this regard were raised before the Commission
also during the hearing of the petition which the Commission had rejected
on the grounds that these were new contentions which did not form part
of the petition. It is pointed out that the Appellant had raised these
contentions in its rejoinder filed before the Commission which fact has
been overlooked by the Commission while passing the impugned order.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 11 of 33

19. We have already extracted hereinabove the prayers made by the
Appellant in this petition before the Commission. Since the Performance
Bank Guarantee had not been encashed till the date of the filing of the
petition, no prayer was made for refund of the Bank Guarantee amount.
As already indicated hereinabove, the 2nd Respondent had encashed the
Bank Guarantees amounting to Rs.15 crores during the pendency of the
petition before the Commission. In these circumstances, the Appellant
ought to have amended the petition in order to incorporate these
subsequent events in the petition and to make additional prayer in the
petition with regards to the refund of the Bank Guarantee amount from
the 2nd Respondent. Merely, mentioning about the subsequent events in
the rejoinder, without seeking amendment of petition including the prayer
clause, did not suffice the requirement of law and, therefore, the
Commission was right in rejecting such prayer of the Appellant as it was
manifestly beyond the pleadings.
20. As discussed hereinabove, Article 14 of the PPA provides for
extension of the COD of the solar power project beyond the scheduled
24 months from the date of signing of the PPA upto 34 months albeit with
certain conditions which have been elaborated in paragraph No. 16
hereinabove and are not repeated here for the sake of brevity. Therefore,
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 12 of 33

no fault can be found with the action of 2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO in
encashing the Performance Bank Guarantee submitted by the Appellant
for the reason that the Appellant, concededly did not commission its
power project, within the timelines as specified under Article 14 of the
PPA. For the encashment of the Performance bank guarantees
submitted by the Appellant, TANGEDCO was not required to show any
loss suffered by it on account of non-commissioning of the power project
by the Appellant. The moment, the delay in commissioning the power
project reached beyond 24 months from the date of signing of the PPA,
the encashment of performance bank guarantee triggered in as per
Article 14 of the PPA.
21. It is only when the delay in commissioning of the power project is
condoned and the SCOD of the project is extended on the request of the
project developer on account of some force majeure event as envisaged
under clause 22 of the PPA that the TANGEDCO may not be entitled to
encash the Performance Bank Guarantee furnished by the Developer. In
the instant case, the TANGEDCO encashed the Bank Guarantee of
Appellant before the plea of Force Majeure set up by Appellant in the
petition, was decided. Such encashment of Bank Guarantee appears to
have been accepted by the Appellant as it neither sought amendment of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 13 of 33

petition including the prayer clause nor filed a fresh petition in this context
challenging the encashment of Bank Guarantee by TANGEDCO.
Therefore, the encashment of Bank Guarantees cannot be assailed in
this appeal when there were no such pleadings raised before the
Commission. Appeal, being the extension of the proceedings before the
Court/Forum below, has to be decided on the basis of
pleadings/contentions raised therein.
22. Hence, we do not find any fault or lacunae in the impugned order
of the Commission on the aspect of encashment of Bank Guarantees of
the Appellant.
23. In so far as the liquidated damages are concerned, whether the
Appellant is liable to pay the same to the 2nd Respondent - TANGEDCO
as per Article 14 of the PPA, as held by the Commission in the impugned
order, it is argued on behalf of the Appellant that Appellant cannot be
asked to pay liquidated damages in the absence of any pleadings or proof
on behalf of the 2nd Respondent that it suffered any loss on account of
non-commissioning of the power project. It is argued that as per well-
settled legal position, a stipulation of liquidated damages in the contract
is a genuine pre-estimate of damages suffered in cases of breach and even
if it is a genuine pre-estimate, there is requirement to prove that actual loss
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 14 of 33

has been suffered by the party seeking liquidated damages. It is argued
that when there is no loss, liquidated damages cannot be granted.
24. Reliance is placed on the judgements of the Hon’ble Supreme
Court in Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das (AIR 1963 SC 1405) and
Murlidhar Chiranjilal vs. Harishchandra Dwarkadas, (1962) 1 SCR 653.
25. It is argued that TANGEDCO neither claimed nor attempted to
prove that any loss has been suffered by it on account of non-
commissioning of the power project by the Appellant and hence, the
Commission erred in proceeding to award damages to it in the absence
of such proof merely on speculative basis.
26. On this aspect, it is argued on behalf of the TANGEDCO that failure
on the part of the Appellant to meet its obligations to commission the
power project and supply power to TANGEDCO resulted in TANGEDCO
having to meet the energy shortfall from other sources which included
thermal power generators. It is argued that it is extremely difficult to
identify and quantify the exact loss suffered by a Distribution Licensees
on account of delay or interruption in power supply under a PPA. It is
pointed out that procurers like TANGEDCO have agreements with a
number of generating stations for procurement of electricity and
additionally, they also have to purchase power from exchanges to meet
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 15 of 33

demand fluctuations during particular times of the day and if a seller or
a generating company fails to supply power or delays in supplying power
from the agreed date, it is extremely difficult to ascertain the exact
replacing source and to compute the cost difference in a linear fashion
unlike other transactions involving movable goods. In this regard,
reliance is placed upon the previous judgement of this Tribunal dated 12th
January, 2015 in Lanco Kondopalli Power Ltd. vs. APERC in Appeal No.
154 of 2013.
27. The primary argument advanced on behalf of the appellant is that
since the 2nd respondent has failed to prove that it suffered any loss on
account of non-commissioning of the power project by the Appellant
within the stipulated timeline, the Commission has erred in granting
compensation to the 2nd respondent as liquidated damages. The
argument is based upon Sections 73 and 74 of the Indian Contract Act,
1872 which are quoted hereinbelow: -
“73. Compensation for loss or damage
caused by breach of contract.—When a
contract has been broken, the party who suffers
by such breach is entitled to receive, from the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 16 of 33

party who has broken the contract,
compensation for any loss or damage caused to
him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual
course of things from such breach, or which the
parties knew, when they made the contract, to
be likely to result from the breach of it. Such
compensation is not to be given for any remote
and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason
of the breach.
Compensation for failure to discharge
obligation resembling those created by
contract.—When an obligation resembling
those created by contract has been incurred and
has not been discharged, any person injured by
the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the
same compensation from the party in default, as
if such person had contracted to discharge it and
had broken his contract.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 17 of 33

Explanation.—In estimating the loss or damage
arising from a breach of contract, the means
which existed of remedying the inconvenience
caused by the non-performance of the contract
must be taken into account.
74. Compensation for breach of contract
where penalty stipulated for.— When a
contract has been broken, if a sum is named in
the contract as the amount to be paid in case of
such breach, or if the contract contains any other
stipulation by way of penalty, the party
complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or
not actual damage or loss is proved to have
been caused thereby, to receive from the party
who has broken the contract reasonable
compensation not exceeding the amount so
named or, as the case may be, the penalty
stipulated for.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 18 of 33

Explanation.—A stipulation for increased
interest from the date of default may be a
stipulation by way of penalty.
Exception.—When any person enters into any
bail-bond, recognizance or other instrument of
the same nature, or, under the provisions of any
law, or under the orders of the Central
Government or of any State Government, gives
any bond for the performance of any public duty
or act in which the public are interested, he shall
be liable, upon breach of the condition of any
such instrument, to pay the whole sum
mentioned therein.
Explanation.—A person who enters into a
contract with Government does not necessarily
thereby undertake any public duty, or promise to
do an act in which the public are interested.”
28. Section 73 of the Contract Act embodies the general principle with
regards to assessment of damages caused by the breach of contract and
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 19 of 33

provides that the compensation would be payable by the party
committing the breach for the damages caused to the other party, which
damage was anticipated by parties to be likely to occur in case of the
breach of the agreement or which arose naturally in the usual course of
things from such breach. Section 74 speaks of the measure of damages
to be awarded in case of breach of contract where the contract itself
specifies any amount to be paid in case of such breach or contains any
other stipulation by way of penalty. In both the cases the measure of
damages is reasonable compensation, not exceeding the amounts so
specified in the contract or the penalty stipulated for, whether or not actual
damage or loss is proved to have been caused by the breach.
29. Bare perusal of Section 74 would reveal that parties are free to
stipulate any amount in the agreement that will be paid by the party who
commits breach of the terms of the agreement i.e. defaulting party to the
other party in the agreement. It further provides that the amount of
liquidated damages so fixed in the agreement would be the maximum
amount payable by the defaulting party and the court will not allow more
than that amount fixed in the contract but may award a smaller amount
depending upon the facts and circumstance of the case. In other words,
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 20 of 33

the court would award only a reasonable amount of liquidated damages
even though the same are pre-estimated and spelt out in advance in the
contract.
30. The Hon’ble Supreme Court has interpreted Section 74 of the
Contract Act in a catena of judgements and the latest one being Kailash
Nath Associates v. DDA & Anr. (2015) 4 SCC 136, the relevant
paragraphs of which are reproduced hereunder: -
“33. Section 74 occurs in Chapter 6 of the Indian
Contract Act, 1872 which reads "Of the
consequences of breach of contract". It is in fact
sandwiched between Sections 73 and 75 which
deal with compensation for loss or damage
caused by breach of contract and compensation
for damage which a party may sustain through
non-fulfillment of a contract after such party
rightfully rescinds such contract. It is important
to note that like Sections 73 and 75,
compensation is payable for breach of contract
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 21 of 33

under Section 74 only where damage or loss is
caused by such breach.”
“43. On a conspectus of the above authorities,
the law on compensation for breach of contract
under Section 74 can be stated to be as follows:-
43.1 Where a sum is named in a contract as a
liquidated amount payable by way of damages,
the party complaining of a breach can receive as
reasonable compensation such liquidated
amount only if it is a genuine preestimate of
damages fixed by both parties and found to be
such by the Court. In other cases, where a sum
is named in a contract as a liquidated amount
payable by way of damages, only reasonable
compensation can be awarded not exceeding
the amount so stated. Similarly, in cases where
the amount fixed is in the nature of penalty, only
reasonable compensation can be awarded not
exceeding the penalty so stated. In both cases,
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

the liquidated amount or penalty is the upper
limit beyond which the Court cannot grant
reasonable compensation.
43.2 Reasonable compensation will be fixed on
well known principles that are applicable to the
law of contract, which are to be found inter alia
in Section 73 of the Contract Act.
43.3 Since Section 74 awards reasonable
compensation for damage or loss caused by a
breach of contract, damage or loss caused is a
sine qua non for the applicability of the Section.
43.4 The Section applies whether a person is a
plaintiff or a defendant in a suit.
43.5 The sum spoken of may already be paid or
be payable in future.

43.6 The expression "whether or not actual

31. Thus, any damage or loss suffered by a party due to breach of
contract on the part of another party to the contract is a sine qua non for
applicability of this section i.e. for award of liquidated damages. Even if a
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

sum of money is stipulated in the contract as liquidated amount payable
by the defaulting party by way of damages, only reasonable
compensation commensurate with the loss/damages suffered by the
other party, can be awarded not exceeding the amount so specified in
the contract.
32. In Maula Bux v. Union of India (1969) 2 SCC 544, the Apex court
has held as under:-
6. … … … Reliance in support of this contention
was placed upon the expression (used in
Section 74 of the Contract Act), "the party
complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or
not actual damage or loss is proved to have

breach of contract the person aggrieved by the

even if no actual damage is proved to have been

caused thereby" is intended to cover different
classes of contracts which come before the

may be impossible for the Court to assess

other cases compensation can be calculated in
accordance with established rules. Where the
Court is unable to assess the compensation, the

nature of a penalty. Where loss in terms of
money can be determined, the party claiming

compensation must prove the loss suffered by

“10. Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act deals
with the measure of damages in two classes of
cases (i) where the contract names a sum to be
paid in case of breach and `ii) where the contract
contains any other stipulation by way of penalty.

decide whether a contract containing a covenant
of forfeiture of deposit for due performance of a
contract falls within the first class. The measure
of damages in the case of breach of a stipulation
by way of penalty is by Section 74 reasonable
compensation not exceeding the penalty
stipulated for. In assessing damages the Court
has, subject to the limit of the penalty stipulated,
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 27 of 33

jurisdiction to award such compensation as it
deems reasonable having regard to all the
circumstances of tile case. Jurisdiction of the
Court to award compensation in case of breach

maximum stipulated; but compensation has to
be reasonable, and that imposes upon the Court
duty to award compensation according to settled
principles. The section undoubtedly says that
the aggrieved party is entitled to receive
compensation from the party who has broken
the contract, whether or not actual damage or

of contract can be awarded to make good loss
or damage which naturally arose in the usual
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 28 of 33

15. Section 74 declares the law as to liability
upon breach of contract where compensation is
by agreement of the parties predetermined, or
where there is a stipulation by way of penalty.
But the application of the enactment is not
restricted to cases where the aggrieved party
claims relief' as a plaintiff. The section does not
confer a special benefit upon any party; it merely
declares the law that notwithstanding any term
in the contract predetermining damages or
providing for forfeiture of any property by way of
penalty, the court will award to the party
aggrieved only reasonable compensation not
exceeding the amount named or penalty
stipulated. The jurisdiction of the court is not
determined by the accidental circumstance of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 29 of 33

the party in default being a plaintiff or a
defendant in a suit. Use of the expression "to
receive from the party who has broken the
contract" does not predicate that the jurisdiction
of the court to adjust amounts which have been
paid by the party in default cannot be exercised
in dealing with the claim of the party complaining
of breach of contract. The court has to adjudge
in every case reasonable compensation to
which the plaintiff is entitled from the defendant
on breach of the contract. Such compensation
has to be ascertained having regard to the
conditions existing on the date of the breach.”
34. It is thus well settled that the essential ingredients required to be
pleaded and established by a party claiming damages on account of
breach of contract are: -
(a) There has been breach of contract by the other party;
(b) the party complaining of such breach has suffered in injury or
damage as a result of the breach of contract by the other
party; and
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 30 of 33

(c) the injury suffered is proximate and direct result of the breach
committed by the other party.
35. The expression “whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to
have been caused thereby” occurring in Section 74 have been
interpreted to mean that where it is possible to prove actual damage or
loss, such proof is not dispensed with. It is only in cases where damage
or loss is difficult or impossible to prove that the liquidated amount
indicated in the contract, if a genuine pre-estimate of damage or loss, can
be awarded.
36. In the instant case, we find from the perusal of the impugned order
of the Commission that the Commission did not venture to ascertain
whether or not was any loss suffered by TANGEDCO on account of non-
commissioning of the power project by the Appellant within the timeline
as specified in the PPA or on account of non-supply of power by the
Appellant. The Commission ought to have called upon TANGEDCO to
demonstrate that any loss was suffered by it on account of default on the
part of the Appellant in commissioning of the power project within the
specified timeline. There is no assertion of finding in the impugned order
that the case was of such nature where it was impossible on the part of
the TANGEDCO to prove any damage or loss suffered by it and the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 31 of 33

extent of liquidated amount to which it was entitled from the Appellant. In
the absence of any such exercise, the Commission appears to have held
in an arbitrary and cavalier manner that the Respondent No. 2 –
TANGEDCO is entitled to relief provided in clause 14 of the PPA i.e.
liquidated damages from the Appellant to the extent of non-
commissioning of the power project. Therefore, we are of the opinion that
the case deserves to be remanded back to the Commission for fresh
consideration on this aspect.
Conclusion
37. In view of the above discussion, the prayer of the Appellant for
refund of the Bank Guarantee amount is hereby rejected. However, we
set aside the impugned order of the Commission in so far as it holds the
2nd Respondent – TANGEDCO entitled to liquidated damages from the
Appellant in terms of Article 14 of the PPA to the extent of non-
commissioning of the power project by the Appellant. We hereby remand
the case back to the Commission for fresh consideration on the aspect
and to decide, upon hearing both the parties, whether or not had the
TANGEDCO suffered any loss on account of non-commissioning of the
power project by the Appellant within the timelines specified in the PPA
and if so, to what extent. Thereafter, the liability of the Appellant to pay
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 151 of 2021 Page 32 of 33

liquidated damages to TANGEDCO in terms of Article 14 of the PPA shall
be ascertained.
38. The appeal stands partly allowed to the extent indicated
hereinabove.
